Text | Zhihan Guo

Editors | Er Mu, Fanyu Meng

Imagine walking down a street and hearing a bird singing in the treetops overhead. Even though you can’t see it through the thick leaves, you can roughly tell how far away it is. Then a bicycle bell rings behind you, coming closer, and without turning around you step aside to let it pass. Everyday moments like these show that, without help from our eyes, our ears and brain can perceive how far away a source is from sound alone. For that to work, sound must carry some information, or cues, that help us judge distance.

Generally speaking, human distance perception is very inaccurate. The dividing line lies at about one meter: when a source is closer than that, people tend to perceive it as farther away than it actually is, and when it is more than a meter away, its distance is underestimated.

Average estimated distance (n = 5 participants) as a function of physical source distance. The results are well approximated by a compressive power function with an exponent of 0.45 and a multiplicative constant of 1.17 [1].

As the plot shows, auditory distance perception is reliable only when the source is close to the listener. As the source moves away, perceived distance seems to be “compressed.” When a source is ten meters away, for example, it is hard to judge its distance at all accurately from sound alone: the auditory stimulus it produces is very similar to that of a source eight or twelve meters away.

Auditory cues that affect distance perception

Any piece of audio contains a number of acoustic cues that can be used to perceive the distance between listener and source. This section summarizes several widely accepted cues that influence distance perception.

Sound pressure level (SPL)

Sound pressure level is the level of a sound’s pressure, expressed in decibels (dB). SPL has long been treated as the main acoustic cue for distance perception, because in most situations it is considered usable. Under ideal conditions (a source of constant sound power in a free field), the relationship between SPL and source–receiver distance follows the inverse square law: each doubling of distance lowers the SPL by about 6 dB. Our brain uses this relationship to estimate distance from how loud a sound is.

Interestingly, research shows that the type of source (noise or speech, for instance) and its angular position (directly facing the listener or at 90 degrees, say) also strongly affect how much weight we give SPL as a distance cue [2]. In other words, depending on the situation, we may rely more or less on SPL to perceive distance.

Direct-to-reverberant energy ratio (DRR)

Indoors, sound waves from a source can travel straight to our ears (the direct sound) or reach them after reflecting off walls, the ceiling, the floor and other surfaces (the reverberant sound). The DRR is the ratio of the direct-sound energy reaching our ears to the reverberant energy. One open question is how to define the direct-sound energy. It is generally taken as the sum of the sound energy from the direct-sound peak over a short period afterwards, but researchers use different durations for the direct sound, ranging from 1.5 ms [3] to 8 ms [4]. The reverberant energy is then all the sound energy from the end of the direct sound to the end of the impulse response.

An impulse response measured in a room. The red arrow marks the direct-sound peak; the blue box shows the range over which the direct-sound energy is calculated.

Reverberation makes it harder to localize the direction of a source [5] but helps with distance perception [6], because the DRR carries useful information. Because of the way reverberant sound is distributed in a space, its energy is fairly uniform throughout the room. Changing the distance between source and receiver therefore has relatively little effect on the reverberant sound. The energy of the direct sound, however, decays exponentially with distance, so at a receiver farther from the source the reverberant sound makes up a larger share relative to the direct sound. The DRR thus decreases as the distance between listener and source increases, and from this change we can roughly judge how far away the source is.

Spectrum

In audio and signal processing, the spectrum describes how a signal or sound is distributed in the frequency domain. Analyzing a signal’s spectrum reveals the relative strength of its frequency components. As sound travels through air, higher frequencies are attenuated more than lower ones, which changes the shape of the spectrum. Note that the spectrum can serve as a cue only when the listener is more than 15 m from the source [7]. Within 15 m, spectral cues carry no distance information, because the sound has not traveled far enough to lose a perceptible amount of high-frequency energy, and the low-frequency cues from diffraction around the head are too small to detect [8].

Figure a shows the spectra of the room impulse responses measured at 2 m and 8 m at the same angle. Figure b shows the difference between the 2 m and 8 m spectra together with a linear fit: the spectral difference grows slightly with frequency.

Binaural cues

Differences between what our two ears receive are a key cue for locating sound sources. They include the interaural level difference (ILD), the interaural time difference (ITD) and the head-related transfer function (HRTF), which together help us determine the direction and distance of a source.

When a source is close to the listener, the level difference between the two ears is large. For a source within one meter of the head and off to one side, a change in distance can change the ILD by as much as 20 dB. If the source is straight ahead of the listener, however, the paths to the left and right ears are symmetrical, so the ILD is tiny and provides no distance information [9]. Beyond one meter, the ILD becomes roughly independent of source distance [10]. The ITD, by contrast, varies less dramatically with the distance of a nearby source than the ILD does, and so contributes less to distance judgments.

HRTF parallax refers to changes in the HRTF caused by the different distances between each of the listener’s ears and the source, and it too can be used to determine the distance of sources relatively close to the listener. Acoustic parallax occurs when a sound is fairly close to the head, so that the angle of the source relative to the left ear differs from its angle relative to the right ear. For a source in front of the listener, the parallax angle grows as the source comes closer, so HRTF parallax can explain how listeners can tell the distance of a nearby source even without ILD and ITD cues [11].

Summary

In this article we explored the importance of binaural hearing for distance perception and described in detail how four key parameters affect it: sound pressure level, the direct-to-reverberant energy ratio, the spectrum and binaural differences. SPL and DRR work at any distance; the spectrum helps only when the source is far from the listener; and binaural differences contribute only when the source is very close. The spectrum and binaural differences therefore have a narrower range of application than SPL and DRR.

Beyond these four parameters, other cues also help us judge distance, such as dynamic cues and familiarity with the source. Understanding how these parameters shape auditory distance perception deepens our understanding of how the human auditory system extracts spatial information in complex acoustic environments. In the future, this knowledge will help improve hearing devices, design more natural audio for virtual reality, and optimize sound system design.

About the author: Zhihan Guo is a master’s student in acoustics at DTU (Technical University of Denmark), mainly interested in psychoacoustics and auralization.
